questions.question: What are the three evaluation layers in eval-driven agent development?
options: Unit, Integration, End-to-end
Static benchmarks, Custom offline evals, Online production evals
Development, Staging, Production
Manual, Automated, Continuous
questions.explanation: The three layers: static benchmarks (SWE-bench, GAIA, WebArena for cross-model comparison), custom offline evals (LLM-as-judge, execution-based, trajectory-based on your product shape), and online evals (session replays, guardrail alerts, per-step cost/latency).

questions.question: What is the 2026 best practice for where evals live?
options: In a separate evaluation repository managed by the QA team
Next to the code, run in CI on every PR, gating merge on eval scores
In a shared Google Sheet updated weekly
Only in production monitoring, not in development
questions.explanation: 2026 best practice: evals live next to code, run in CI on every PR, gate merge on eval scores (e.g., no regression >5% vs main), map every guardrail to an eval case, map every learned rule to a failure case.

questions.question: What is the 'no baseline' failure mode in eval-driven development?
options: Not having any evals at all
Having evals without a last-known-good reference score, making regression detection impossible
Running evals only once per release
Using evals that are too easy
questions.explanation: Without a baseline (last-known-good score), evals are unreadable — you cannot tell if a 75% pass rate is an improvement or a regression. Store baselines and compare every run against them.

questions.question: What does Anthropic's guidance say about when to add multi-agent complexity?
options: Add it from the start to avoid refactoring
Start with simple prompts, optimize with comprehensive evaluation, add multi-step agentic systems only when needed
Add it whenever team size exceeds 5 engineers
Only add it for tasks with user-facing latency requirements
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance: 'start with simple prompts, optimize them with comprehensive evaluation, and add multi-step agentic systems only when needed.' Evaluation is the outer loop that drives every other choice — not the last step.

questions.question: What is the 'over-fitting to evals' failure mode?
options: Writing too many eval cases
Optimizing the system specifically for eval metrics in ways that diverge from production usefulness
Running evals too frequently
Using eval scores as the primary development metric
questions.explanation: Over-fitting to evals means optimizing the agent specifically for the evaluation metrics in ways that don't transfer to production. Mitigation: rotate eval cases, add new cases from production failures, keep evals representative of real usage.

questions.question: What Phase 14 lesson connects to the eval case 'PVE refuses poisoned retrievals'?
options: Lesson 05 (Self-Refine and CRITIC)
Lesson 27 (Prompt Injection Defense)
Lesson 06 (Tool Use)
Lesson 13 (LangGraph)
questions.explanation: The eval case 'PVE refuses poisoned retrievals' connects to Lesson 27 (Prompt Injection Defense), which teaches the Prompt-Validator-Executor pattern for detecting and blocking prompt injection attempts in retrieved content.
